description_full: TOYO Co., Ltd. engages in the upstream production of wafer and silicon, midstream production of solar cell, downstream production of photovoltaic (PV) modules, and other stages of the solar power supply chain in Asia and the United States. It designs, manufactures, and sells solar cells, modules, and related products. TOYO Co., Ltd. was founded in 2022 and is headquartered in Tokyo, Japan.
ceo_bio: Mr. Takahiko  Onozuka | Chairman & CEO | Age 64
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 2K people. Revenue per employee of $167K ranks in the bottom quartile among Technology peers. Each employee generates $16K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $4K per employee reflects an ownership culture.
financial_summary: TOYO Co., Ltd is a micro-cap technology business with a $229M market cap on $427M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +142% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +8.8pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.

Returns on capital run at 26% against a 9% cost of capital — a 17-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 17% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $41M in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.35× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -21.1% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.0× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 18× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 76% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 69% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 93% and a beta of 0.80, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 2.29 vs 5y 0.17), so read it loosely.

prof: ROIC of 26% clears the cost of capital of 8.7% by 17pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.87).

Earnings quality is mixed: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 3.35x, but high accruals (-21.1% of assets).
ROE of 36% is amplified by 4.0x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.

hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.0x net debt to EBITDA ($103.5M of cash against $114.6M of debt), with interest covered 17.8x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.78 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.

growth: At current returns, reinvesting 2% of profits supports about 0.6% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Capex runs 2.5x depreciation (21.5% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
It has missed earnings estimates by 4.6% on average.
